So on the US vs China thing, there's one major difference which makes all the difference when it comes to equities markets etc. It's WAYYY harder to fudge the numbers here, and there's no centralized force that has a stake in making it possible. Our government agencies won't simply make up employment, export, energy reserve, GDP numbers etc. There are too many smart financial institutions with access to enough data to call bullshit if they had to. Our markets work on data which is generally accurate, if slightly massaged, because there is no way to get away with faking it for too long, and the penalties for doing so are massive. Jump into the world of financial and economic data for a bit, if just for your own edification. There are detailed weekly reports on everything which move markets here in the US.

China on the other hand? They have an extremely managed economy, which is directly connected to the political leverage of the Chinese government. The CCP's power globally, as well as domestically, is tied inexorably to their ability to convince people that their economy is growing at the alarming rate they say it is. They also have unlimited power to coerce every sector of industry in that country to fit their agenda, especially since the leaders/owners of the large concerns in China are usually high ranking CCP members. Therefor, no individual in the financial world trusts data out of China, because their political power and economy are linked in such a way that they have both the incentive and means to manipulate their markets and data.

What this means in terms of Chinese stock markets complicates things even further, because unlike in the US where most major players in equities markets are financial institutions, in China they are predominantly retail investors (normal ass people), and unsophisticated ones at that. CCP ran state media had been encouraging everyone in China to buy stocks, with an implicit promise that it was essentially free money, using the same fake data they try to pass off to everyone else. The problem is, once the securities market drops a bit, the unsophisticated investors are most likely to panic sell, and in China, that's most of the investors.

Now on to FIAT currencies. Just because you quizzed me, I'll touch on this. Yes, we left the gold standard in 1973 (it was 73, right?), but that doesn't mean we should go back to it now. Our dollar is pegged to oil now, and frankly, the price of crude in global markets is far more relevant than the price of gold these days. I don't personally mind the federal reserve playing with the money supply if they can achieve the goals necessary to keep the economy growing steadily. Everyone's assumption is that the printing of new money "out of thin air" will lead to runaway inflation, but the truth is that we're currently fighting deflation, and potentially stagflation if equities markets have another flat year in 2016. The fed has raised the interest rates on new money recently, and IMO that was a good move, and signals a move back to a more sustainable monetary policy. Whatever gets us to around 2% inflation is what we need to do. 2% is a healthy figure.
